blocks.b:
Jim Marshall taught and played drums around London, and by 1960 he wanted a steadier living. He opened a shop, still mostly drums, called Jim and Terry Marshall at 76 Uxbridge Road, Hanwell. By 1962 a second shop had opened across the road, and the business had become J&T Marshall.

His drum pupils brought their guitarists in, among them Ritchie Blackmore, Jimmy Page and Pete Townshend. They told him they would rather buy guitars and amplifiers from him, because the West End shops treated them “like absolute idiots” for playing rock and roll.

Britain had kept American instruments out through the 1950s, and the big Fender amplifiers his customers wanted were scarce. Marshall imported what he could, but demand far outran supply. He turned to his repair technician Ken Bran, a guitarist he had hired from a repair job at Pan Am, and they chose Fender's late-1950s tweed Bassman, the 5F6-A, as the model.

Accounts differ on whether they copied a borrowed amplifier or worked from the schematic. An apprentice engineer from EMI helped with the design. The first prototype, late in 1962, followed the circuit closely but used British transformers, capacitors and resistors, and it brought in dozens of orders. Marshall recalled building amplifiers from Monday to Friday to sell in the shop on Saturday.

On the earliest heads the chassis was pushed to one end of the cabinet, and the front was covered in the same salt-and-pepper Vynair as the speaker grilles. The badge was a metal plate with MARSHALL in red enamel. It came from a Birmingham supplier of funeral goods, and it is still known as the coffin badge.

Inside, they copied the Bassman closely enough to keep its polarity switch, made for ungrounded American outlets and useless on British three-pin plugs. They kept its 5881 output valves. In the preamp they used the ECC83, the European 12AX7, in place of Fender's 12AY7. Each gave about two and a half times the gain, and the amplifier distorted sooner.

The production amplifiers of 1963 had the panel in the centre. Later that year came the sandwich front, with a black stripe across the top third. The polarity switch went and the panel read JTM 45 and MK II. The output valves later changed to British-made KT66s. Heads were sold as lead, bass and PA models, all essentially the same circuit.

By the end of 1963 the front was all black. The badge gave way to a silver Plexiglas plate with red letters, then to black letters on gold, and in 1965 to the script logo Marshall still uses. Panels of Traffolyte or aluminium gave way to Plexiglas the same year, first white, then gold. The head at the top of this chapter is a 1965 amplifier with the gold block logo.

Marshall built heads first and cabinets later. He recalled starting with two-by-twelves, but the 25-watt speakers of the day could not take an amplifier that peaked at around 70 watts, and they blew. He designed the smallest cabinet that would hold four 12-inch speakers. The first were Celestion G12 alnicos rated at 15 watts each. The ceramic G12M Greenback, at 20 watts, arrived in 1965 and was raised to 25 watts in 1968.

The cabinet was closed at the back, which gave a midrange punch unlike Fender's open-back combos. Dave Hunter, in The British Amp Invasion, calls the head on its 4x12 “the mightiest thing on the British stage” in 1963.

In 1964 Marshall added two combos built around the JTM45: the Model 1961 Super Tremolo with four 10-inch speakers, and the Model 1962 Lead and Bass with two 12s. In May 1966 Eric Clapton recorded with John Mayall's Bluesbreakers at Decca's studios in West Hampstead, playing a 1960 Les Paul through a Model 1962. The album came out in July, and the combo has been called the Bluesbreaker since.

The story that Clapton wanted an amp that fitted in the boot of his car is very likely false, since the combos were on sale before he used one. Which amp he played is not recorded, and Clapton has said he did not know what became of it.

By mid-1965 Pete Townshend's Fender amplifiers were not loud enough for the Who, and he asked Marshall for more. The JTM45/100 prototypes ran two 30-watt output transformers in parallel and a pair of GZ34 rectifiers, then a pair of 50-watt Drake transformers and four KT66s. The Who took several 100-watt heads in November 1965, with at least four cabinets holding eight 12-inch speakers each.

The eight-by-twelves soon gave way to two 4x12 cabinets, a straight one below and an angled one above. The 100-watt head became the Model 1959.

blocks.b:
Leo Fender never learned to play the guitar. He lost a job as an accountant in the Depression, had been repairing radios since he was 14, and opened the Fender Radio and Record Shop in Fullerton, California, where he also fixed amplifiers. After the single-speaker Champ and Deluxe, Fender added the Twin in 1952, first listed as the Twin 12 Amplifier and the Twin 12 Artist's Model.

The first version, the 5C8, had two 12-inch Jensen speakers and a pair of 6L6 output valves, and was rated at 25 watts. Its tweed cabinet had a new wide-panel front, with the grille cloth running between the inside edges of the box, and Fender called it its new “Hi Fidelity” amplifier.

Narrow-panel cabinets followed, with only thin strips of wood above and below the baffle. Dave Hunter, writing in Guitar & Bass, calls the early Twins “really just siblings of the Super and Pro amps”, with the same circuit and two 12-inch speakers, and notes that players who wanted more power often chose a Bassman.

By 1957 and 1958 the Twin used the 5E8A circuit, rated first at 40 and then at 80 watts. It ran two 5U4 rectifier valves, an unusual layout that reduced sag on hard-picked notes. Hunter says the tweed Twins are closer in sound and circuit to an early Marshall Bluesbreaker than to the Twin most players know today.

The tweed gave way to Tolex at the start of the 1960s. In 1961 the Twin came in white Tolex with a maroon grille cloth, with volume, treble and bass on the normal channel and volume, treble, bass, speed and intensity on the vibrato channel. A wheat grille arrived toward the end of 1962, and early in 1963 a black metal-reinforced handle replaced the brown one. Collectors still date these amps by their covering, grille and handle.

The Twin Reverb was introduced in late summer 1963. It was rated at 85 watts and had a silver-sparkle grille, a raised Fender logo and a new two-channel circuit, with bright switches on both channels in place of a presence control. The middle control came back, and the numbered, skirted knobs sat on a black panel, which is where the name blackface comes from.

The new features were spring reverb and a control Fender labelled vibrato. It varied the volume rather than the pitch, so it was a tremolo. The tweed and blonde Twins had different circuits and no reverb at all.

Hunter calls the blackface Twin Reverb “the benchmark design”, the most powerful large professional guitar amplifier then sold by a major maker. Where other Fenders began to break up at about 4 on the volume knob, a Twin Reverb stayed clean to about 6 or 7. That suited bands playing big stages without microphones on the amps, and it left a clean base for effects pedals. The amplifier weighed 35 kilograms or more.

It could still roar when it was turned up. Michael Bloomfield played a blackface Twin Reverb on his recordings with the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, photographs from the 1960s show Keith Richards with blackface Twin Reverbs, and the Beatles used Twin Reverbs for the Apple rooftop performance.

Leo Fender sold the company to CBS in 1965. The silverface Twin Reverb followed in late 1967 or 1968, depending on the account, with a brushed aluminium panel and a blue-sparkle grille. The early silverface circuit changed the bias and phase inverter and added seven parts to the output stage, and the rating rose to 100 watts.

A master volume arrived in 1972, and the rating reached 135 watts in 1977. Harry Hank of Hank's Vintage Guitars says the master volume and boost controls turned the clean amp with lots of headroom into a dirtier, less responsive one. The black panel returned as an option in 1980 and was standard by 1982, the last year of the traditional Twin Reverb. Fender later reissued the 1965 version.

blocks.b: The front and back panels of Marshall’s 100-watt head were cut from gold acrylic sheet, and players named the amplifier the Plexi after the Plexiglas brand, though Marshall's acrylic was not made by Plexiglas. In 1966 Marshall signed a fifteen-year distribution deal with Rose-Morris, and the distributor gave the head the model number 1959. It is a catalogue number, not a year.

Inside, it is a plain amplifier. It has two channels, Normal and Bright, and no gain control, effects loop, channel switching or reverb. Every original was wired by hand. Marshall did not move to printed circuit boards until 1973.

The first 100-watt heads of late 1965 used the JTM45's preamp and its gold front panel, with a white rear panel reading Super 100 Amplifier. Their two 50-watt Drake output transformers gave way to a single 100-watt Drake, introduced in September 1965, so the dual-transformer heads are rare. Power transformers, voltages and chokes kept changing, and Jim Marshall told Nick Bowcott that some changes simply followed which parts were available.

The Jimi Hendrix Experience and Cream used these early heads heavily in 1966 and 1967. Hendrix's full name was James Marshall Hendrix, and he went to meet Jim Marshall after hearing the amplifiers in England. When he asked for a more “toppy” or aggressive sound, the amplifiers were adjusted. Marshall called him “my greatest ambassador without any doubt at all.”

In February 1967 Marshall fitted a new Drake output transformer and four EL34 power valves. The amplifier became louder and sounded dirtier and more aggressive.

In the late spring of 1967 gold acrylic back panels reading Super Lead and Super Bass were introduced, while the JTM45 front panel stayed. The Super Lead gained a 500 pF bright capacitor in its preamp. The Super Bass, Model 1992, used the same circuit without it.

In mid-1967 the chassis changed from aluminium to steel, which was sturdier and cheaper to make. A reversed JTM logo appeared on the front panel beside the power and standby switches. These heads, made only briefly, are called Black Flag amplifiers.

Later in 1967 the logo became three black capitals, JMP, for Jim Marshall Products. In 1968 the preamp was rebuilt around a split-cathode circuit, which changed the tone of both channels and made the amplifier louder and tighter. Later that year larger filter values tightened the bass.

In 1969 a resistor change in the Bright channel gave it a crisper tone that cleaned up well. The Marshall historian Mike Doyle lists Jimmy Page, Jimi Hendrix and Eric Johnson among the players of this version.

The best-known Super Lead built in 1968 belonged to Edward Van Halen, who used it on Van Halen's first albums, beginning with the band's debut in 1978. It is often said to have been modified.

Bowcott writes that it was stock. Van Halen lowered its mains voltage with a Variac, which makes the preamp and the power stage distort earlier and gives the amplifier a softer response.

In mid-1969 Marshall replaced the acrylic panels with aluminium. The circuit stayed the same for a while, and the Super Lead name and the 1959 number stayed with the amplifier. Judas Priest, Thin Lizzy and AC/DC played the aluminium-panel heads through the 1970s, and printed circuit boards replaced the hand wiring in 1973.

Marshall reissued the Plexi in 1993 as the 1959SLP, on circuit boards and based on an amplifier from late 1968 or early 1969. The 1959SLPX followed in the early 2000s with a series effects loop. The hand-wired 1959HW came in 2005, modelled on two original heads, one of them 60 serial numbers from the heads Hendrix played at Woodstock in 1969.

blocks.b:
Ivor Arbiter was an amateur drummer who opened Drum City on Shaftesbury Avenue in London in the late 1950s. By 1966 his company had three shops in the West End, among them Sound City on Rupert Street, which sold guitars and amplifiers. In the early 1960s he sold Ringo Starr a Ludwig Black Oyster Pearl kit and drew the Beatles logo with the dropped T on the bass drum himself.

In the autumn of 1966 Arbiter Electronics put the Fuzz Face on sale. The advertisement promised "the ultimate in controlled effects".

The circuit had two transistors, four resistors, three capacitors and two controls, Fuzz and Volume. It is almost identical to the Sola Sound Tone Bender Mk 1.5, and the Fuzz Face instruction sheet called it a battery-powered tone bending unit. The footswitch was a double-pole, double-throw type, which took the circuit out of the signal path completely when it was off.

Denis Cornell, who later tested the pedals, remembered Arbiter's account: he used the bottom of a microphone stand to hold the circuit board, and the case stayed round. The two knobs were the eyes, the footswitch the nose, and the cut-out badge reading Arbiter England the smile.

A Maestro Fuzz-Tone cost £30 in Britain. The Fuzz Face cost £6. Jimi Hendrix arrived in London on 24 September 1966 and spent time at Sound City, which distributed Fender guitars and lent equipment to the Jimi Hendrix Experience. In November 1966 he was photographed using a Fuzz Face at the Big Apple club in Munich.

Hendrix's technician Roger Mayer said the band had 15 or 20 Fuzz Faces and lost three or four a week. Mayer built better fuzz boxes for Hendrix within two months, and those stayed off the road; the cheap Arbiter pedals went to gigs.

The early pedals used germanium transistors, most often the NKT275 made by Newmarket in England. Their gain varied from one transistor to the next and drifted with temperature, and the circuit only sounded right with a balanced pair. Mayer said you might buy 20 pedals to find a good one, and a good one could still sound worse on a different day.

Cornell called the testing "a nightmare". Voltage readings and an oscilloscope did not show the differences, so he plugged in a guitar, struck a note and listened to the decay. Weak units died away quickly and lost the high notes. In a good one the note sustained.

The input impedance is low, so the pedal reacts to the guitar's pickups. Turning the guitar's volume knob down lowers the gain until the sound is almost clean.

After money problems, Arbiter merged with Dallas Musical, in 1967 by one account and 1968 by the other, and around 1968 the badge changed to Dallas Arbiter England. Painted lettering gave way to decals in about 1970, and a light blue finish appeared around 1969.

In 1968 and 1969 the NKT275 was replaced by silicon transistors, first the BC108C and then the BC183L, later the BC109C and BC209C. Silicon was cheaper and less affected by heat, and it gave more distortion. It also picked up AM radio. "When you connected the Fuzz Face to a guitar cable, the cable acted like a bloody antenna," Mayer said, and on stage stations came through Hendrix's amplifiers.

In the studio Mayer rarely ran a Fuzz Face straight from the guitar. He put buffers with different equalisation in front of it so that it saw a low-impedance source, changed the voltage it ran on, and added EQ before and after the fuzz. In his words, one simple device would not get the tone Hendrix got on a record.

The original Fuzz Face went out of production in 1974 or 1975; the two accounts differ. A final batch followed in 1976 or 1977. In 1986 Dave Fox, a technician at Crest Audio in New Jersey, the company Dallas had bought, revived the pedal with matched BC109C silicon transistors, using a blue 1970s unit from the stockroom to make a new mould. About 2,000 were made in grey, blue and red, with the badge printed on a sticker.

At the 1987 NAMM show Fox found Dunlop selling a black Jimi Hendrix Fuzz. Dunlop and Crest reached an agreement, and in 1993 Dunlop bought the Dallas Arbiter and Fuzz Face names. In the late 1990s Arbiter's company asked Cornell to make a run of the original design, but only about the first 100 were built.

blocks.b:
The wah pedal came out of another project. In 1966 Vox's American team was designing the Super Beatle, a transistor version of the AC50 made only for the US market, with reverb and a mid-range boost called MRB. They found that the boosted frequency could be swept with the volume pedal from a Vox Continental organ. To them it sounded like a trumpet player working a mute.

The effect is a band-pass filter with a sharp resonant peak, moved up and down by the foot.

Thomas Organ, which made and sold Vox products in the United States, finished its first wah pedal in late 1966 and named it after Clyde McCoy, a jazz trumpeter known for playing with a cup mute. His picture was on the bottom of the pedal. It went into the Vox Ampliphonic line for band and orchestra and was aimed at amplified brass and woodwind players, not guitarists.

At a press conference reported by Billboard on 8 April 1967, Vox said the real market for the wah was the guitar. The company dropped Clyde McCoy and renamed the pedal the V846 Vox Wah-Wah. Print advertisements for guitarists began in May 1967, and a 60-second radio commercial featured the Electric Prunes.

Eric Clapton, Jimi Hendrix, Jimmy Page and George Harrison took it up, as did Terry Kath of Chicago, Martin Barre of Jethro Tull and Tony Iommi of Black Sabbath.

Thomas Organ built the first V846 pedals in Sepulveda, California, in early 1967. By the middle of the year production had moved to EME, the Eko guitar company, in Recanati, Italy, and about a year later to JEN in Pescara. In the early 1970s JEN and Thomas Organ in California shared the work. When the California plant closed in the late 1970s, JEN and the Thomas International Corporation plant in Chicago made the pedal.

Thomas began production in 1957, so adding 57 to the first two digits of a serial number usually gives the year. An Italian pedal numbered 1631067 dates from 1973, and an American one numbered 1995087 from 1976.

Every Clyde McCoy, V846, King Wah and Cry Baby was built from the same schematic, but they do not sound the same. Most of the difference comes from two parts. The first is the 500 mH ferrite-core inductor, which came from five suppliers. All had the same value, but their cores saturated differently and added different harmonics. The Clyde McCoy and many early V846s used the Halo, named after the silver ring that holds it together. Italian pedals from EME and JEN often had the Trash Can, and some 1970s JEN pedals a Fasel.

The second is the 100 kΩ pot. A pinion gear on its shaft meshes with a toothed rack under the rocker, turning the up-and-down movement of the foot into rotation. The Italian pedals used an ICAR pot with a taper between linear and audio, and many have since failed.

The footswitch is single-pole, so a 0.01 µF capacitor stays in the signal even when the wah is off and takes away some treble.

In 1971 Miles Davis used a wah pedal on his trumpet for the album Live-Evil, after seeing Jimi Hendrix play. A pedal designed to make a guitar sound like a muted trumpet was now making a trumpet sound like a guitar.

Vox still makes the V846, along with the hand-wired V846-HW on a turret board and the V847C with a lower sweep and more gain.

blocks.b:
Engineers found soon after the Second World War that a reel-to-reel tape recorder could play a sound back a moment after recording it. A short slapback echo, often mixed with reverb, became part of early rock and roll records. From the 1950s inventors built the idea into small portable machines with a short loop of tape. Musicians liked them, but they did not survive the road well, and some used valves that were often unreliable.

Roland was founded in 1972. In 1973 it added its first Space Echo units, the RE-100 and RE-200, and in 1974 replaced them with the RE-101 and RE-201. Both were cheaper than rival echo units, heavily built and able to take several kinds of input. The RE-201 had more features, and it became the one musicians and studio engineers wanted.

The tape transport sat under a hinged lid on top of the cabinet. Earlier portable machines stretched a short loop over reels, like a small reel-to-reel recorder, and the tape wore quickly under constant tension. The RE-201 used one long loop that spooled loosely into a chamber under a clear plastic cover. With less tension the tape lasted longer, and the length allowed echoes of more than three seconds.

The tape stopped moving whenever the bypass footswitch was pressed, which saved more wear. The electronics were solid-state and kept background noise low.

The loop ran past one record head and three playback heads, driven by a motor whose speed could be varied. The Repeat Rate knob changed the tape speed and with it the delay time. The 12-position Mode Selector picked one playback head or several, and several heads together gave a multi-tap pattern of echoes. Intensity set how much of the delayed sound went back to the record head, and so how many repeats followed. A spring reverb was built in and could be used alone or with the echoes.

The front panel also had bass and treble controls for the effect, separate echo and reverb levels, two microphone inputs and an instrument input, each with its own volume control, and an input for a mixer.

The RE-201 was used on tour and in recording studios, and Roland says it has been heard on thousands of records. Its echoes faded behind the original sound as they repeated, so they sat easily in a mix. Turning Repeat Rate and Intensity while a signal was playing pushed the machine into oscillation and pitch shifts. Because the input level control also set the level of the dry signal, guitarists used the Space Echo to drive the front end of a valve amplifier.

Roland's list of users includes Lee “Scratch” Perry, King Tubby, Brian Eno, Pink Floyd, Hank Marvin of the Shadows, Randy Rhoads, Sonic Youth and Radiohead.

The RE-301 of 1977 kept the spring reverb and added a chorus circuit. Its erase head could be switched off, so sounds could be layered on the tape. The RE-150 of 1979 used the same tape system without reverb. In 1980 Roland introduced the RE-501, with balanced inputs and outputs, remote control options, delay, reverb and chorus, and the SRE-555, a rackmount version of it.

Digital delays were becoming affordable by the late 1980s. Roland released the RE-5 Digital Space Echo in 1987 and the RE-3 in 1988. They used no tape and were lighter and more consistent, but they did not reproduce the tape units exactly. BOSS dates the end of RE-201 production to 1988, and Roland Australia to 1990.

Many original RE-201s are still in use and sell for high prices, but replacement parts have become hard to find. In 2007 BOSS released the RE-20, a twin pedal that models the RE-201 with its COSM technology, including tape saturation, the preamp and the wow and flutter of the transport. Its Mode Selector and knobs follow the original panel. Turning Repeat Rate bends the pitch of the echoes until the modelled tape speed settles, as on the original. The RE-20 also doubled the longest delay to six seconds and added stereo inputs and outputs.

In 2022 BOSS released the RE-202 and the compact RE-2, after its engineers studied several original RE-201s. Each original sounds different depending on its tape and how hard the preamp is driven, so the RE-202 lets the player set tape age, saturation and wow and flutter.

blocks.b:
Most drive pedals of the mid-1970s were fuzzes, such as the Maestro FZ-1, the Fuzz Face, the Tone Bender and the Big Muff. Played hard, they tended to blur the low strings. Boss, Roland's effects brand, began its compact pedal series in 1977 with the OD-1 Overdrive, the PH-1 Phaser and the SP-1 Spectrum, which Boss now calls the traffic light pedals after their yellow, green and red cases.

The OD-1 used asymmetrical clipping to imitate a valve amplifier starting to break up. According to Boss, its engineers next set out to build a full distortion that improved on what was already on the market.

The DS-1 Distortion joined the compact series in 1978 as its fourth pedal, in an orange case. A Japanese collector who has studied Boss serial numbers dates the first production run to June 1978. It has three controls, Tone, Level and Dist, over a single footswitch.

The ProCo RAT appeared the same year. Both used diodes to clip the signal hard, and their more saturated sound helped make distortion and overdrive separate categories. The DS-1 has stayed in the Boss catalogue since 1978, and Boss says it has sold more than 1.5 million, more than any other pedal in the compact series.

The signal passes a transistor gain stage, then an integrated-circuit stage with much more gain, and then a pair of diodes that cut the peaks flat. Boss describes this as the two common drive designs of the time combined in one hard-clipping circuit. Hard clipping produces more upper harmonics than the soft clipping of an overdrive.

The Tone knob is a tilt control. One way it adds bass and removes treble, the other way it does the opposite, and there is no flat setting. The voicing also dips slightly in the lower midrange. Through a mid-heavy amplifier such as a Marshall or a tweed Fender the dip is filled in, and through a scooped blackface or silverface Fender the pedal can sound thin.

Jack Endino, who recorded Nirvana's debut Bleach in 1989, told Guitar World that Kurt Cobain's sound that year came from a DS-1. After Surfing with the Alien became a hit in 1987, Joe Satriani had to tour without the money for vintage Marshalls and decided “to get the sound in a little box”, the DS-1. Steve Vai's technician Thomas Nordegg said it was Vai's main pedal from 1999.

George Lynch of Dokken has used one since the 1980s, and the jazz guitarist Mike Stern said he used it on every one of his own records. Boss also lists John Frusciante on the Red Hot Chili Peppers' Stadium Arcadium and Mark Speer of Khruangbin.

The DS-1 was cheap, easy to find and built on a simple board, so it became one of the most modified pedals. Boss names Analog Man and Robert Keeley among the best-known modders. Most mods add low end by changing the coupling capacitors, smooth the treble that hard clipping creates, raise the output, or swap the clipping diodes. Keeley's Ultra mod became one of the best known.

The first DS-1s used a Toshiba TA7136 preamplifier chip, and these are often described as the warmest and smoothest. Boss moved production from Japan to Taiwan around 1989 and 1990. In 1994, with the Toshiba chip running out, it rebuilt the circuit around a Rohm BA728N dual op-amp and called it the DS-1A. Early Japanese pedals have a silver thumbscrew on the battery door, and later ones a black one.

The DS-2 Turbo Distortion followed in 1987. In 1998 Boss gave a small run of gold DS-1s to distributors and top dealers to mark six million compact pedals sold, and it calls them the rarest Boss pedals. The DS-1X came in 2014, the black DS-1-4A for the 40th anniversary in 2018, and the Japanese-built DS-1W Waza Craft, with Standard and Custom modes, in 2022.

blocks.b:
ProCo began in Kalamazoo, Michigan, in 1974. A group of music businesses called the Sound Factory closed that year, and the next day Charlie Wicks, who had run its music shop, started ProCo Sound. The company first made speaker cabinets with Electro-Voice, along with microphone and guitar cables and stage snakes.

Kalamazoo lies halfway between Chicago and Detroit, so touring bands often stopped there between dates. It was also a college town where the drinking age was 18, and it already had a busy music scene in 1974.

An engineer named Scott Burnham designed the RAT circuit in 1977 or 1978, possibly from an idea he had in 1974. His official job title was Hippie in Charge of Technology. He and another engineer, Steve Kiraly, had been repairing and modifying distortion pedals for years, and Burnham said he had listened to all of them and liked none.

While he worked on the circuit in ProCo's basement, which had rats, Burnham fitted a resistor of the wrong value in the op-amp's gain stage. The op-amp overloaded and clipped against its supply rails, and the sound was one he had never heard before.

The first RATs were built into plain project boxes from Bud Industries, ordered from a catalogue, and are known as Bud Box RATs. They are usually dated to 1978, though Burnham recently dated one lent to a Kalamazoo museum exhibit to 1977. It is often said that he made twelve. He built twelve circuits but put them into eleven pedals, one of them a double unit for a man named Tom Taylor, and they were sold to order.

A ProCo product sheet lists the Bud Box RAT as an official product, although it was never made in quantity. It may have been drawn up to pitch the idea to Wicks.

Wicks agreed to put the RAT into full production in the 1979 catalogue. The first production version, released early in 1979, is called the Fringe Logo RAT after the lines branching off its lettering. It came in a larger 20-gauge wrap-around case, which gave the early pedals the name Big Box RAT, with controls for Distortion, Tone and Volume. Hundreds carried left-over serial labels printed for the Systech 4001 Flanger, made by a company that had shared the building.

Later in 1979 the logo was redrawn and the knobs changed twice. By the end of the year the RAT had black plastic knobs with a white line. The circuit stayed the same.

In 1981 the Tone control became a Filter control. Two lugs of the pot were swapped, so turning it clockwise now cut treble instead of adding it. The component values did not change.

By 1984 Boss, Ibanez, DOD and MXR sold pedals in cases half the size, and RAT sales were falling. ProCo moved it into a small box with a white block logo, and in 1986 redrew the logo in thin lines because the white ink smudged in printing.

The RAT2 of 1988 added a status LED, through a bypass circuit attributed to Steve Kiraly, and a Lexan overlay with glow-in-the-dark graphics. Its distortion circuit was the same as in 1981, though customers wrote in to say it sounded different.

In 1989 an employee named Gerry Carpenter, known as Grape, replaced the RAT's silicon clipping diodes with red LEDs from ProCo's stock. With the gain down and the volume up it worked as an overdrive in front of his already distorted Marshall. Wicks had the Turbo RAT on sale within six months, and in 1991 ProCo reissued the Big Box.

Texas Instruments declared the RAT's LM308 op-amp obsolete in 1993. Carpenter chose the OP07DP as a replacement, and RAT2s made after 1996 use it. Around 2008 Neutrik began building the RAT2 in its Chinese factory in a sloped case, while the other RAT models stayed in the United States.

blocks.b:
In 1908 the Hoshino Shoten bookshop opened in Nagoya, Japan, selling books and sheet music. It soon sold musical instruments as well, through a new division called Hoshino Gakki Ten, and in 1929 began importing Spanish guitars made by the luthier Salvador Ibáñez. By 1935 Hoshino was building the guitars itself, and in 1957 it shortened the name to create the Ibanez brand.

By the 1960s Ibanez was known for high-quality copies of Fender, Gibson and Rickenbacker guitars, the years now called the lawsuit era.

In the 1970s Ibanez added effects pedals, made by Nisshin Onpa, a Japanese company founded in 1971 that had built some of its pickups. Nisshin Onpa designed and built the pedals, Ibanez sold them under its name, and Nisshin Onpa sold the same pedals under its own brand, Maxon, without the international distribution Ibanez had. From 1979 to 2002 Maxon made the Tube Screamer.

Maxon's Susumu Tamura designed it, and it reached the market as the Ibanez TS808 and the Maxon OD808 at the same time. Tamura wanted a softer distortion that added sustain and harmonics while keeping the guitar's own tone. The pedal shipped in 1979 but did not appear in the Ibanez price list until May 1980, at $50. Early sales were weak.

A valve amplifier clips the top and bottom of the waveform unequally. Roland's Boss held a patent on solid-state asymmetrical clipping, so Maxon used symmetrical clipping, which is generally smoother. John Lomas, a former Ibanez product manager, said the schematics of the Tube Screamer and the Boss OD-1 were almost the same. The TS808 added a tone control, a small footswitch and a JRC 4558D op-amp chip, and Lomas said it was the first overdrive he had seen built around an integrated circuit rather than transistors.

Tamura said the name came from Sammy Ash, grandson of the founder of Sam Ash music stores, whom he visited on West 48th Street in Manhattan before the launch. When they tried the pedal through an amplifier, Ash said it sounded like a screaming tube amp.

The company that made the TS808's small footswitch stopped producing it, so the pedal was redesigned. The TS9 of 1982 had a larger switch, a slightly brighter sound and more output, and sales improved. A 1984 price list shows it at $75.

The first TS9s, made from 1982 to 1984, used parts from various suppliers, and units varied widely in tone. As the yen weakened against the dollar in the mid-1980s, Ibanez had to make its pedals more cheaply, and the first-run TS9 was dropped by 1985. In 1986 Ibanez released the TS10 Tube Screamer Classic, the first Tube Screamer built in Taiwan rather than by Maxon.

Interest in the old pedals grew through the recordings of Stevie Ray Vaughan, beginning with Texas Flood in 1983. He used a TS808 early on, then mostly TS9s through the 1980s, and moved to the TS10 in 1988. He used it as a boost, with the level turned up and the overdrive set low to push the front of his amplifiers. His guitar technician René Martinez has said Vaughan favoured the TS10.

Trey Anastasio runs two TS9s at different settings, Kirk Hammett uses one to push the midrange for solos, The Edge for a light bite, and Eric Johnson keeps a TS808 with the tone turned all the way down.

In 1991 Ibanez launched the Soundtank series, including a TS5 in a plastic case. Lomas spent time convincing Ibanez and Maxon that a TS9 reissue would sell. Maxon bought up vintage TS9s and found that almost all had a Toshiba TA75558 chip rather than the JRC, so the reissue used the Toshiba part. It was built in Japan in the same factory as the originals, with a reprint of the 1981 manual in the box, and more than 5,000 sold within weeks.

The four-knob TS9DX Turbo Tube Screamer followed in 1998. In 2002 Ibanez stopped using Maxon, which kept making the pedals under its own name. The TS808 reissue came out in 2004 and the hand-wired TS808HW in 2008.

blocks.b:
Marshall's fifteen-year distribution deal with Rose-Morris ran out in 1981. Jim Marshall took over distribution himself and used the change to launch a new range. At its core the JCM800 was a cosmetic redesign of the existing Master Volume models, with a gold panel, black grille cloth with white piping and Jim's signature across the front.

The Master Volume series dated from 1975, when Marshall was already known as the Dukes of Distortion. It answered players who wanted the same distorted, sustained sound at lower volume, and it introduced the 100-watt 2203 and the 50-watt 2204. Both were already popular when they joined the JCM800 range.

None of the names suggested for the range quite fitted, so Jim Marshall used the number plate of his own car. JCM were his initials, for James Charles Marshall. The 800 meant nothing in particular, and the range arrived at the start of a new decade.

Under the new styling was the Master Volume circuit of the late-1970s 2203 and 2204, which gave a powerful overdriven sound at practical volume. The 100-watt 2203 came to define the range. It had one channel, no reverb, a preamp volume, a master volume and a three-band EQ. In the mid-1980s changes to the reservoir capacitors gave later amplifiers a tighter, more aggressive response with less sag and compression.

The range kept growing. The 4210 combo of 1982 added reverb, channel switching and front-facing controls that were easier to reach on stage, and the two-channel 2205 and 2210 heads followed in 1983.

The 2203 became a standard amplifier for rock and metal bands through the 1980s. Kerry King and Jeff Hanneman of Slayer built their thrash sound on it, and Zakk Wylde has used it from his first years with Ozzy Osbourne through Black Label Society.

It was not used only for heavy music. Jeff Beck, Andy Summers of the Police, Joey Santiago of the Pixies and Buddy Guy all played JCM800s, and Lzzy Hale of Halestorm and Lee Malia of Bring Me the Horizon use the 2203 today.

The original series ran until 1990, when the JCM900 replaced it. Marshall brought the 2203 back in 2002 as a Vintage Reissue, built at its factory in Bletchley and faithful to the original apart from an added series effects loop. It is still made, alongside the 20-watt Studio Classic, a smaller version, and the JCM800 Modified, which adds gain and tonal range.

blocks.b:
Paul Reed Smith spent about ten years building custom guitars, for Carlos Santana, Ted Nugent and Peter Frampton among others. In 1985, on the strength of orders from a sales trip and the Winter NAMM show, he moved into a factory on Virginia Avenue in Annapolis, Maryland. The first guitars with serial numbers came off the line in August 1985, when 18 people worked there.

By December 2019 PRS employed more than 300 people and made about 1,800 guitars a month. The Custom 24 was its first model.

Smith told Guitar Player in 1982 that the whole idea was to understand why the old Les Pauls were great guitars. The Custom had a one-piece mahogany neck glued into a one-piece mahogany body, with a carved maple top whose edge was left unpainted instead of bound in plastic. Its 25-inch scale sat between the 25½ inches of most Fenders and the 24¾ of many Gibsons, so that both Strat players and Les Paul players might take to it.

An attempt to average the outlines of a Strat and a Les Paul Junior looked horrible, Smith said, so he drew a new shape, which took about two years. The all-mahogany version was simply the Paul Reed Smith guitar until 1987, when it became the Standard. Most buyers wanted the maple top.

A five-way rotary switch gave the humbucking sounds and split-coil sounds close to a Stratocaster. There was no tone control. A Sweet switch imitated the treble loss of a 104-foot guitar cable, reportedly at Santana's request when he moved from long cables to a wireless system. The fingerboards were Brazilian rosewood.

Santana's commission had sent Smith looking for ways to keep a Strat-style vibrato in tune. He built the first PRS vibrato with John Mann, an engineer and guitarist: a single casting of plate and block on six notched pivot screws, with a push-in arm that could not snap off like a screw-in Strat arm. A nylon and Teflon nut and PRS locking tuners, developed with Eric Pritchard, completed the system.

The first review appeared in Guitar Player in April 1986, written by the luthier Rick Turner, who said he had not played an electric guitar he liked better. A fully loaded Custom with bird inlays and a Brazilian rosewood fingerboard listed at $1,550. That year a Gibson Les Paul Standard listed at $995 and an American vintage-style Stratocaster at $750.

Fender opened its Custom Shop in 1987, and Gibson formalised its own in 1993. PRS was building production guitars to custom-shop standards before either, and it brought a new guitar design to market that sold. Tom Johnston of the Doobie Brothers and David Grissom were among the early players.

In October 1987 the switch's middle position changed from both humbuckers to a series Strat sound using the two inside coils. By 1991 the pickups were HFS and Vintage Bass, and the fingerboards changed to Indian rosewood. The Custom 22 arrived in 1993, and the original was renamed the Custom 24. That year brought a second-generation vibrato with a separate plate and block, and a dual-action truss rod.

In the mid-1990s computer-assisted machines took over the rough cutting and shaping of necks and bodies. In 1995 PRS moved to a new plant in Stevensville, Maryland. Sales had grown from half a million dollars in the first year to $10 million, and the Private Stock shop began building guitars to customers' designs.

The Custom 24 stayed the best-selling guitar in the line. Tim Mahoney of 311 played stop-tail Custom 24s from the mid-1990s, Brad Delson of Linkin Park used one on stage around 2000, and in 2005 Dave Navarro got the first Custom 24 signature model, PRS's third signature guitar after Santana and Mark Tremonti.

A new factory about five times the size of the first building opened in 2009. In 2011 the rotary switch gave way to a five-way blade, in 2015 the pickups became the 85/15 design, and in 2017 the Custom 24-08 added separate mini switches for each pickup.

blocks.b:
By the mid-1980s the market was full of superstrats, and Kramer had Eddie Van Halen. Ibanez had worked with Lee Ritenour, Joe Pass, Steve Lukather and Allan Holdsworth, but had no rock headliner. In 1986 Hoshino's Joe Hoshino called a meeting at the distribution centre outside Philadelphia and said Ibanez needed its own Eddie Van Halen. According to Bill Reim, later president of Hoshino USA, everyone in the room said more or less at once that it had to be Steve Vai.

Vai had joined Frank Zappa's touring band in 1980 at 20, replaced Yngwie Malmsteen in Alcatrazz in 1984, and by the end of 1985 was playing with David Lee Roth.

Ibanez reached Vai through his mother on Long Island and had a guitar placed under the tree at his parents' house for Christmas 1986. Vai sent Ibanez guitars with notes on the features he liked, and Mace Bailey built prototypes from them. Vai said Ibanez took three weeks to give him exactly what he wanted. Fujigen built the JEM777 in time for the summer NAMM show of 1987, the first time it had used basswood bodies.

At NAMM the stand sat under a black shroud with a guard beside it. On the second day it was unveiled with a poster of Vai, who jumped on stage holding the guitar. The first 777 limited Loch Ness Green JEMs listed at $1,590 and sold out within a month.

Ibanez released the RG550 at the same show, as a more affordable JEM. It was first part of the Roadstar Deluxe series, which became the RG series. It kept the JEM's basswood body, with its slim horns and squared edges, but dropped the monkey grip handle and the lion's claw tremolo rout, partly to save cost. Pyramid inlays gave way to dots, and the DiMarzios to American-designed Ibanez V1, S1 and V2 pickups in a humbucker, single-coil, humbucker layout.

The one-piece maple Wizard neck was only 17 mm deep at the nut, thin enough to need a new kind of truss rod. It had 24 jumbo frets on a 25½-inch scale, a joint giving easy access to the top frets, and a double-locking Edge tremolo. It was made in Japan.

The first finishes included Road Flare, Desert Sun Yellow and White. Until 1989 the fingerboard could be maple or rosewood, and after that it was maple. In 1990 the volume pot moved further from the bridge pickup so the tremolo arm would not hit it. From 1992 the RG550 had a Lo-Pro Edge tremolo and a quartersawn maple neck, and in 1994 it gained the AANJ neck joint and V7 and V8 pickups. It listed at $749.95 in 1990 and $899.95 in 1993.

The original RG550 was dropped after 1994 and a new one appeared in 1997. For the RG series' twentieth anniversary in 2007 Ibanez reissued the 1987 guitar, and in 2013 Japan got a limited Genesis Collection version.

The RG sold in the thousands in its first year. Players took to its fast neck and stable tremolo, among them Paul Gilbert of Mr. Big, Dave Navarro of Jane's Addiction, Wes Borland of Limp Bizkit and John Petrucci of Dream Theater. Seven-string RGs followed in 1998, and the first eight-string, the RG2228, in 2007. Today the RG line has more than 60 models, from the Japanese Prestige series to the entry-level GIO.

blocks.b:
In the 1980s Bill Finnegan played in bands around Boston with a Telecaster plugged straight into a Twin Reverb. In bigger clubs he could run the amp at seven and liked the sound. In smaller ones the sound engineer turned him down to three or four, and the amplifier lost the harmonic richness it had when it was working hard.

Around 1990 guitarists were looking for vintage Tube Screamers, and Finnegan bought a couple of TS9s. He said the TS9 compressed the attack of the note, had a midrange character he disliked and took away a noticeable amount of bass. He wanted a more open sound with a touch of valve-like clipping, from a pedal that would not make him aware it was there.

He recruited a friend who had recently graduated from MIT, and since both had day jobs they met once a week. The first prototypes came within a year, and Boston guitarists who tried them urged him to go into production, but Finnegan thought the circuit could still improve. When his partner moved away he found another MIT graduate, Fred Fenning, who was neither a musician nor an audio engineer but was good at making the circuit do what Finnegan imagined. Finnegan credits Fenning with much of the final design.

The work took four and a half years. The Centaur went on sale in 1994 at $225.

Finnegan built, tested and shipped every Centaur himself, at a folding table in a series of small apartments in Boston, working 55 to 60 hours a week. The cast enclosure, knobs, pots and bottom plate were all custom-made, and he estimates a Centaur cost seven or eight times as much to produce as an ordinary pedal of the time. For its last seven or eight years it sold for $329, still on a thin margin, and Boston rents ruled out a proper workshop.

Over about fifteen years he built around 8,000 by hand. Buyers waited 12 to 14 weeks, used prices kept rising, and in 2009 the Centaur went out of production.

The Gain knob turns two stacked pots that blend clipped signal with clean. Fully down it is a clean boost; fully up the clean signal is gone. A charge pump raises the internal supply from 9 to 18 volts for more headroom, a separate path carries the lows to the output, and a high-quality buffer sits at the input.

Around 1993 and 1994 Finnegan chose 1N34A germanium diodes, which sounded more natural to him than silicon. Before the internet, he found a distributor that had been left with a large stock decades earlier and bought all of it. The diodes clip on top of a TL072 op-amp stage. Finnegan covered the boards in epoxy, which fed rumours that the Centaur was a modified copy of something else, until the circuit was traced and published around 2007.

In 2008 Finnegan began moving the design to one that could be made in a conventional factory. He spent two years listening to surface-mount capacitors in different parts of the circuit before he was satisfied. The result was the KTR, with the same circuit and the same germanium diodes in a much smaller case, built by an outside manufacturer. Its production also quietly stopped.

Meanwhile copies multiplied, among them the Electro-Harmonix Soul Food, the J. Rockett Archer, the Wampler Tumnus, the Keeley Oxblood and the Mythos Mjolnir. Finnegan has argued that copying a circuit without paying its designer discourages anyone from building something new.

Jeff Beck, John Mayer, Warren Haynes, Jim Campilongo and Nels Cline have all used Centaurs, and original units have sold for as much as $5,000. Finnegan's advice is that the pedal is an overdrive, so the amplifier, of any size, should already be turned up to the point where it begins to break up.

In February 2019 Finnegan began building a few Centaurs again from original enclosures and parts, selling them one at a time at auction on eBay. The first was listed at $100 and sold for $2,026.

blocks.b:
Christoph Kemper is an electrical engineer from Bochum, in the old coal and steel region of Germany, which is why the Kemper logo carries a mining tower. He wrote audio filter algorithms out of personal interest, and in 1995 he rented a rotary speaker, set it up in his living room, studied how it behaved and built a digital model of it.

He said he could not play guitar, but that had not stopped him modelling what was, in effect, an amplifier and a speaker.

Kemper joined the founder of a company called Access, which made remote controllers for synthesizers, and their first product was the Access Virus synthesizer of 1997. The Virus was accepted as a convincing model of analogue synths and went on stage with bands such as Depeche Mode.

Guitar modelling products of the time, Kemper said, stayed mostly in hotel rooms for practice and demos. He thought something was wrong there, talked to many guitarists, and in 2006 turned to developing guitar products.

Modelling copies the behaviour of electronic circuits, and the engineers decide what the perfect Plexi or AC30 should sound like. Kemper wanted players to bring their own sound into the digital domain instead. The Profiler sends test signals at different frequencies into the player's amplifier, records the result through a microphone on the cabinet, and builds what Kemper calls a fingerprint of the rig. The player can then adjust qualities such as compression, power-amp sag and pick attack.

The Profiler uses a Motorola DSP, now made by NXP, which Kemper programs himself.

Kemper imagined an amplifier in a lunchbox that could sit on a speaker cabinet or on a studio desk, so the panel is tilted, the signal path shows on the front, and a row of knobs follows the controls of a valve amp. The team came from synthesizers, where players want as many physical controls as possible, and Kemper said that if you make a guitar amp you had better have a Gain knob.

The Profiler was shown at the NAMM Show in 2011, as a head and a rack unit, with a floor controller called the Profiler Remote. The original has a green metal chassis with grey front panels, and a version with a 600-watt power amp followed.

Most owners play profiles made by others. Professional vendors offer thousands for free, and tens of thousands more are shared on Kemper's Rig Exchange. New features arrive as free firmware updates, a practice Kemper began with the Virus in 1998. Players include Steve Winwood, Steve Morse, Paul Gilbert and Pat Metheny.

Guitar World later called the Profiler polarising at its release but much improved by its software. The Profiler Stage floorboard and the stompbox-sized Profiler Player followed, Liquid Profiling arrived in 2023 to let a profile follow the tone controls of a modelled amp, and in 2025 Kemper announced an MK 2 version of the whole line.

Ola Strandberg built guitars as a hobby from childhood. He studied mechanical engineering, and his first job was in a workshop, doing metalwork and CAD drawings, before his career moved to designing administrative software and then to product management.

The guitars stayed a hobby until a midlife crisis sent him back to building them, this time with years of experience in how products are designed, made and managed.

The guitar that had first caught his attention was Allan Holdsworth's, made of jelutong. He was also taken with the headless designs Steinberger made in the 1980s, but he wanted an instrument that balanced better on the strap and a neck that let the wrist and hand stay in a natural position.

In 2007 he built a prototype in secret, in the basement workshop of the biotech company he worked for. Once he showed it online it drew interest, and he went on building guitars one at a time. Holdsworth later received one of them.

In 2012 came the EndurNeck. Instead of a rounded back, the neck has flat surfaces in an asymmetric trapezoid, an idea Strandberg took from a TV remote. A hand grips something thick more strongly, so the profile changes along its length to suit the shape the hand takes for chords at one end and for solos at the other.

Strandberg says players used to both thick and thin necks find it comfortable, and that it keeps the wrist straighter, with less stress, less fatigue and fewer injuries. Players with repetitive strain injuries have reported that it helped them. The shape is patented and used only on Strandberg guitars.

After the EndurNeck, Strandberg founded the company in Sweden, with its headquarters in Uppsala. The guitars were designed headless from the start rather than adapted from a conventional body, which gave them less weight, better balance and steadier tuning.

Finding a manufacturer who could build them took time, and the first mass-produced batch arrived in 2014.

The Boden became the flagship. MusicRadar compared its body to a puddle drawn by Dalí, and Guitar World credited Strandberg with a boom in headless guitars that brought models from Ibanez, Schecter and Kiesel.

In progressive metal the Boden became a common choice, and Plini, Jacob Collier and Jordan Rudess play Strandbergs. In 2025 Guitar World included the Boden in its list of the 50 greatest pieces of gear of the century.
